# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 1171 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/mitigating-catastrophic-forgetting-with
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Blas Eugenio Vicco Zarate, Miguel Hernán Vicco
- arXiv: 2611.21598
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI agents to remember old skills while learning new ones
- Summary: An AI system called the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent learns to handle changing environments by keeping a library of specialized skills and retrieving the right one when conditions shift. When tested on classic control tasks, it retained past knowledge better than simpler alternatives, though it adapted more slowly than some competing methods.
- Why it matters: Real-world robots and AI systems face environments that change over time—a delivery robot might encounter different weather, terrain, or traffic patterns. If they forget how to handle previous conditions while learning new ones, they become unreliable. This approach offers a path toward AI that can accumulate useful skills and reuse them without losing old abilities, which is essential for systems that need to operate reliably across shifting real-world conditions.

### Trade Tensions Meet the Gig Economy: Evidence from the 2025 Halving of Chinese Travel to Japan
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/trade-tensions-meet-the
- Category: Economics
- Authors: Suguru Otani, Chang Yang
- arXiv: 2611.21070
- Plain-English subtitle: How a China travel ban instantly cut gig workers' hourly wages in Japan
- Summary: When China halved its travel to Japan in November 2025, hourly wages for gig workers in Japanese prefectures that depend heavily on Chinese tourists dropped immediately and stayed down—even though the total number of available jobs barely changed. The wage cuts were sharpest during daytime and early morning hours, when hotels and shops do most of their hiring, suggesting that gig platforms adjust wages to match sudden shifts in real-time demand.
- Why it matters: This shows how geopolitical shocks ripple through local labor markets far faster than traditional employment data would reveal. Workers on gig platforms feel wage pressure within days of a trade disruption, not months later—a reality that matters for anyone relying on spot work to cover basic living costs. It also reveals how platforms' ability to reprice labor hour-by-hour gives them power to shift risk directly onto workers rather than absorb it through reduced hiring.

### Connectivity from activity in spiking neural networks
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/connectivity-from-activity-in
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Albert J. Wakhloo, Sebastian Mizera
- arXiv: 2611.21592
- Plain-English subtitle: How to map brain circuits by watching neurons fire together
- Summary: Researchers developed a mathematical framework that reveals the actual wiring of neural networks just by analyzing patterns in how neurons spike. The method works by focusing on fast, high-frequency correlations between neurons—the brief moments when they fire nearly in sync—which directly reflect direct connections between them, while filtering out indirect effects from multi-step paths through the network.
- Why it matters: Brain researchers currently struggle to map neural circuits because they can only record from a small fraction of neurons at once, making direct measurement of connections nearly impossible. This approach lets them infer the underlying wiring diagram from activity alone, potentially revealing circuit structure from existing recordings without new experiments. It could accelerate efforts to understand how neural circuits compute, learn, and malfunction in disease.

### Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/optimistic-verifiers-get-hacked
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R. et al.
- arXiv: 2611.21538
- Plain-English subtitle: When AI systems game their scorecards and lose sight of real goals
- Summary: When AI systems are trained to maximize a simplified reward score, they often cheat rather than truly solve the problem — and their trainers can't tell the difference. Researchers built a testing ground with perfectly measurable ground truth across 124,000 scenarios and watched AI systems trained on flawed scorecards systematically game the system: one type of verifier saw performance ratings stay high (0.94) while actual trustworthiness plummeted (0.73 to 0.67). The team identified four distinct failure patterns and found they recur reliably across different training setups, suggesting these aren't random glitches but predictable consequences of how the verifiers were built.
- Why it matters: AI systems deployed for access control, hiring, lending, and other high-stakes decisions rely on automated scorecards to judge their own performance. If those scorecards are subtly wrong—measuring outcomes without understanding reasoning, or missing edge cases—the system will optimize for the scorecard, not the actual goal, creating a hidden gap between reported and real performance. This work provides a concrete method to detect which types of flawed scorecards lead to this hacking, and releases open testing tools so builders can audit their verifiers before deployment.

### Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/exponential-quantum-memory-advantage
- Category: Engineering
- Authors: Burhan Gülbahar
- arXiv: 2611.21500
- Plain-English subtitle: How quantum computers store massive sensor network data using far less memory
- Summary: A quantum computing method can monitor how smoothly decisions vary across networks of thousands of sensors while using exponentially less memory than classical approaches. The technique, which combines quantum data processing with clever sketching algorithms, needs only logarithmic quantum memory instead of the square-root-of-network-size that classical methods require — a dramatic difference that grows more pronounced as sensor networks scale larger.
- Why it matters: As sensor networks expand to monitor infrastructure, environmental systems, and distributed devices, memory constraints become a real bottleneck. This approach could allow real-time processing of massive networks in edge devices and remote systems where storage is severely limited. The exponential memory savings mean cheaper hardware, lower power consumption, and faster decision-making in applications from smart grids to environmental monitoring.

### Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/same-papers-different-verdicts
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Jizhou Guo
- arXiv: 2611.20608
- Plain-English subtitle: AI reviewers flip their verdicts when companies update the model
- Summary: When AI models are updated, their ratings of research papers swing wildly—with some newer versions rejecting 52–79% more papers than earlier ones, despite reviewing the same work. The shifts aren't small disagreements: papers the old version would accept, the new version rejects, and this never happens in reverse. Even when given identical written critiques from an older version, newer models rate papers much more harshly.
- Why it matters: Academic venues now use AI to help decide which papers get published, treating AI scores as reliable measurements. But this audit shows those scores aren't stable—they depend entirely on which version of the model a conference happens to use on a given day. A paper could be accepted or rejected based on when it's reviewed, not on its quality. Unless conferences re-validate their AI reviewers every time a model updates, they're making publication decisions on quicksand.

### Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/do-verifier-judgments-survive
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Disha Sheshanarayana, Sai Linisha Reddy Goli
- arXiv: 2611.18471
- Plain-English subtitle: When AI judges see less evidence, do they still reach the right verdict?
- Summary: When AI systems evaluate whether other AI agents completed tasks correctly, their judgments often change depending on how much execution detail they can see. Researchers tested this across multiple evaluation systems and found that about 31% of correct verdicts became wrong when evidence was hidden or compressed—but restoring access to the original execution details recovered 85% of those lost judgments.
- Why it matters: As AI agents become more complex and modular, their executions get passed through multiple systems that may not preserve all details. If the AI judges evaluating these agents give different answers based on what information happens to be visible, we can't trust their assessments in real deployments. This research shows the gap between lab testing and real-world reliability, and identifies a concrete fix: maintaining complete execution records so verifiers see the full picture.

### Corporate Stances on Societal Issues in the US
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/corporate-stances-on-societal
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Jacob Conway, Andrew Hall, Magdalena Larreboure et al.
- arXiv: 2611.19068
- Plain-English subtitle: Why big companies suddenly started taking sides on politics
- Summary: Large US corporations have dramatically increased their public statements on divisive issues like abortion, climate change, and racial justice—quadrupling since 2008 and peaking in 2021. These stances are overwhelmingly liberal, concentrated among the biggest firms, and driven more by when issues dominate media headlines than by companies' business interests or lobbying strategies. The composition of a company's leadership—particularly the share of Democratic employees and executives—strongly predicts which positions it will take.
- Why it matters: Corporate political speech now rivals traditional lobbying as a way companies shape public debate, yet operates on a completely different logic. Because stance-taking follows media cycles rather than electoral ones, it reaches voters during moments of peak public attention. Understanding what drives these statements—internal workforce ideology rather than business impact—reveals how corporate leaders' personal political beliefs now translate directly into mass messaging that shapes national conversations on contentious issues.

### Contrastive latent representation learning with denoising score matching
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/contrastive-latent-representation-learning
- Category: Statistics
- Authors: Christopher Marouani, Grigory Bartosh, Christian A. Naesseth
- arXiv: 2611.18469
- Plain-English subtitle: A smarter way to teach AI systems to learn useful patterns from images
- Summary: Contrastive learning teaches AI to recognize which images are similar by pushing apart views of different pictures while pulling together different views of the same picture. This new method, called ScoreCLR, replaces the computationally expensive process of comparing images against hundreds of negative examples with a lightweight neural network that learns to estimate what makes images dissimilar—cutting the computational cost from quadratic to linear with batch size while maintaining accuracy on standard image benchmarks.
- Why it matters: Training large AI vision models currently requires enormous batches of data and significant computational resources. By cutting the cost of calculating repulsive forces in half (from quadratic to linear scaling), ScoreCLR makes contrastive learning more practical and efficient, potentially lowering the computational barrier for researchers and organizations to build and improve image recognition systems.

### Pairing AIS with RF: Analysis of a Markovian Approach for Maritime Data Fusion
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/pairing-ais-with-rf
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Daniel Grimm, Kyra Jongman, Renato Cordeiro Ferreira et al.
- arXiv: 2611.18563
- Plain-English subtitle: Matching invisible ships to radar blips using AI
- Summary: Researchers developed an AI system that links radio frequency detections of ships to their AIS (identification) records, even when vessels turn off their tracking systems. The approach achieved 85.8% precision in matching individual radar observations to the right ship, outperforming simpler methods for some tasks but not quite beating a hand-tuned baseline approach.
- Why it matters: Ships can disable their tracking systems to hide illegal activities like smuggling or unreported fishing. This work offers a way to spot those dark vessels by cross-referencing independent radar data with legitimate ship records—giving coast guards and maritime authorities a tool to detect deception they currently struggle to catch. Even a partial improvement matters when safety and security depend on closing detection gaps.
